activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
story:
Antoine had signed up to volunteer at the food bank table inside the public library, mostly because Cade had dared him to and he hadn't wanted to say no. That had been two weeks ago, on a Tuesday he still thought about when the room got quiet. Now it was Saturday morning, and Mr. De Vries, the librarian who ran the table, was stacking crates of potatoes by the window while the clock ticked toward noon, when the delivery truck would leave.

"Forty more pounds and we fill the bin," Mr. De Vries said. "After that, the truck won't come back until Thursday."

Antoine counted the crates. There were six, and the bin needed eight. Cade sat on the counter, bored already, flipping through a book about World War II tanks. Braden had wandered toward the mystery shelf and was holding up a cover with a sinister-looking lighthouse on it. "You two want to help," Antoine said, "or just visit the library?"

"Can't help," Braden said. "There's no more potatoes. That's the whole problem."

Antoine looked at the crates again. He perspired under his collar, even in the library's cool air, because he remembered something his grandfather had said last summer, out in the country. They had driven past a field where people were bending over the dirt in long rows, and his grandfather had said, "That's gleaning. Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest." A church group had arranged it, he'd said, and the produce went to food banks. Antoine had half listened. Now he turned the idea over: if farms had leftover crops, then somewhere nearby there were potatoes nobody had picked up.

He found Mr. De Vries at the desk. "Do farmers around here ever let people take what's left after harvest?"

Mr. De Vries set down his pen. "Hollis, out past the fairgrounds. He's been calling all week asking if anyone would come glean his potato field before he plows it under. Nobody's answered him." He checked his watch. "But you'd never make it there and back by noon."

"Twenty minutes by bike," Antoine said. "I timed it once."

"You go with an adult," Mr. De Vries said, but he was already reaching for the phone, and after a short call he nodded. "He says come now. Bring whatever you can carry."

Cade stopped reading. "Now? Like right now?"

"Right now," Antoine said.

They rode hard, three bikes rattling down the road past the fairgrounds, and found Mr. Hollis waiting at the gate with burlap sacks. The field looked empty at first, brown and flat, but when Antoine kicked at a mound of dirt, three potatoes rolled out, fat and whole. They filled four sacks in under an hour while their shirts stuck to their backs and Braden complained about his arms.

They skidded back into the library parking lot at 11:52, and the driver of the truck helped them heave the sacks across the rusted hull into the cargo bed. Mr. De Vries watched from the door of the library with his arms crossed, not smiling exactly, but close to it.

"Eight and a half crates," he said. "Half a crate to spare."

Antoine stood there breathing hard, thinking about all those potatoes that would have been plowed under, and about a Tuesday two weeks ago when he could have said no to Cade and hadn't. He still wasn't sure which had been the braver choice.

"Same time next Saturday?" Cade asked, pulling his bike upright.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
Abigail tapped her pencil against the graph paper and counted the percentages a third time. Fifty-two percent Scottish, thirty percent English, twenty-one percent Irish, fourteen percent French, nine percent German. "One hundred and twenty-six," she muttered. "A town can't be one hundred and twenty-six percent anything." The bell would ring in nineteen minutes, and Ms. Do wanted the heritage graphs up on the wall before the open house started.

"You did the math wrong," said Zaid, leaning over from the next desk. He smelled like the orange he'd been peeling under the table, and shreds of peel clung to his sleeve like tiny boots.

"I did it four times." Abigail turned the paper toward him. "The census website gives these numbers for the whole town. Scottish, fifty-two percent. I wrote them down exactly."

Manha slid her chair around, sneakers squeaking on the linoleum. "Maybe the website is broken," she said. "Or maybe ghosts live here too. Ghost origins. Ooooh."

"Manha, we have seventeen minutes."

"Then stop counting and start thinking," Manha said, popping the tab on her juice box with a hiss. "Why would a real number be too big? Something's being counted twice." She took a long slurp, then added, "I'm just saying, my aunt counts herself as both Trinidadian and Indian, and she gets very offended if you make her pick one."

Abigail stared at the paper. Ms. Do walked past, her heels clicking like a metronome, and paused at their table long enough to emphasize one word: "Check the little note under the table, girls and Zaid. The fine print matters." Then she was gone toward the printer, which was grinding out open house banners that smelled like hot plastic.

The fine print was so small Abigail had to hold the sheet almost to her nose. She read it aloud, slowly. "Because the census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, the origin totals add up to more than the country's population."

"So it's not broken," Zaid said. "It's like the town has more origins than residents, because Zaid is Pakistani and also, let's see, a little Irish. My grandmother insists."

"That's exactly it," Abigail said. "Everybody can put down everything they are. So the same person gets counted under Scottish and under Irish, and the town's numbers pile up over a hundred." She grabbed a fresh sheet and drew a quick sketch of the school: stick figures on the roof, the flag, and little labels floating above each kid's head. One stick figure had three labels. Another had one. The labels in her drawing outnumbered the stick figures, and that was the whole secret, sitting there in pencil.

"It's kind of ironic," Manha said, watching her draw. "You panicked because the numbers were too big, but the too-big numbers were the true part. The residence of every single person in that town fits inside it, but the origins overflow."

"Manha, that was almost poetry," Zaid said. "Also, your juice is leaking."

Abigail laughed and moved the juice box away from the graph with one finger while she lettered a title in her best cursive: Our Origins Add Up to More Than 100 Percent, and That's Not a Mistake. Then she wrote, underneath, smaller: Because since 1981, Canadians can report more than one origin on the census.

She taped the graph and the sketch side by side just as Ms. Do called "Thirty seconds, people." Zaid added a doodle of himself wearing a tiny green hat above the Irish label. Manha added a ghost with a label that said Very Scottish.

The bell rang, the hallway filled with parents' coats and voices and the smell of coffee from the staff room, and Ms. Do stopped in front of their wall. She read the title, looked at the stick figures with their floating labels, and said, "This is the one I'm explaining first."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages, so something posted publicly can turn up in search results.
story:
Julia pushed her noodles around the plate while her mother talked about the community bake sale, which Julia had completely forgotten until that exact second. The poster for it still hung on the school noticeboard, and behind it was a wall of faded photos from bake sales going back years, including one of Julia at age eight, grinning over a burnt tray of cookies.

"Mom, who took that picture of me with the terrible cookies?"

"The newspaper lady, remember? It ran in the online edition too."

Julia set down her fork. She had a project due Friday about a natural phenomenon she found interesting, and suddenly she had a new one, though it lived on the internet instead of in the sky. She took her mother's phone, opened a search page, and typed her own name. There she was, eight years old, cookies and all, third result from the top.

"How?" her mother asked, leaning over.

Julia scrolled slowly. She remembered Lucy once saying something in the computer lab about how search engines use automated programs called crawlers to copy and index public web pages. That was why the photo had survived: it lived on a public page, and a crawler had copied it, so it could turn up in search results even years later. It was like the picture had become durable, the opposite of the paper posters that faded on the noticeboard.

"So anyone could find this," Julia said. "Like Prisha's brother in Australia."

"Or Ms. Whitaker," her mother said mildly. "She asked me today whether you'd finished the poster you promised her for the library."

Julia groaned, then laughed. She had promised that poster two weeks ago, assuming it would vanish politely from everyone's memory. Nothing vanished, apparently. On Wednesday she tested her theory, typing Lucy's name into the search bar, and up popped a comment Lucy had left on a pet store website in fifth grade: "I will conquer my fear of hamsters and buy one this year." Lucy had not conquered it. Lucy still climbed onto chairs for hamsters.

At dinner that night Julia told the whole story, phone propped against the salt shaker, and her mother laughed until she had to put her cup down. Afterwards, Julia emailed Ms. Whitaker three possible designs for the library poster, then printed one and pinned it above her desk where she could not possibly forget it again.

On Friday she stood at the library entrance while Ms. Whitaker taped the poster to the glass door. "Nice work," Ms. Whitaker said. "And no crawlers can get it from here." Julia grinned and pulled out her phone to take a picture of it anyway.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: Compound interest is paid on the principal plus all the interest already earned, so the interest itself starts earning interest.
story:
Maelie spread her bank statements across the kitchen table and frowned at them. Mr. Esposito had assigned a project comparing simple and compound interest over five years, and it was due first period tomorrow. Her friend Lyanna had claimed the topic was easy, but the numbers on the page were not cooperating.

"Five years of statements," Maelie muttered, pulling her calculator closer. Her grandmother had opened the savings account for her when she was eight, and Maelie had added nothing to it since. That was the whole point of the project, actually. She remembered sitting in the bank lobby back then, swinging her legs while her grandmother signed papers, too short to see over the desk. The teller had slid a lollipop across the counter, and Maelie had thought that was the only reward for having an account.

She wrote the interest payments from each year in a column. The first year, eight dollars. The second year, more than eight. She stopped, erased, and checked the second figure again. She had deposited nothing, withdrawn nothing, yet the interest itself had grown.

She texted Elyas, who was doing the same project. "My interest payment went UP even though I added nothing. Is my bank wrong?"

His reply came fast. "Mine did that too. Mr. Esposito called ours compound interest. Look at year three."

Maelie looked at year three. Bigger again. She grabbed a fresh sheet and made two columns: one for her account, and one where she calculated what simple interest would pay, the same eight dollars every single year on the original deposit. By year five the two columns had drifted apart like slow walkers on separate paths. The simple column stayed flat and obedient. Her real account climbed, a little steeper each year, because each interest payment was joined by interest on all the interest before it. She wrote it in her own words and tested it against the numbers: it fit. The pattern was approximate for now, she decided, since she had rounded the cents, but the shape of it was unmistakable.

At ten o'clock her mother dissolved a tablet of hot chocolate into two mugs and set one beside the statements. "Solved?"

"Solved," Maelie said. "Simple interest only ever pays on the original money. Mine pays on everything, including interest it already paid me." She taped the last statement into her notebook and closed the cover.

"Read me the last line," her mother said.

Maelie grinned. "By year five, my account beat simple interest by eleven dollars and thirty-six cents."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Looking at the horizon, a fixed distant point, can ease motion sickness because it helps the eyes agree with what the inner ear feels.
story:
Julia had been dreaming about this trip for two months, and now she was actually standing in the airport with her boarding pass in her fist like a golden ticket. At the big window near Gate 14, she and her dad watched a 747 taxi out, and she used his binoculars to magnify it until the plane filled the whole lens, its tail number huge and glorious. "Window seat is mine," she reminded him. They had signed a formal treaty in the car, written on a napkin: Julia got the window, Dad got the armrest, Mom got to pick the snacks. The treaty was notarized with a jelly stain.

Then came security, which was slightly invasive, in Julia's opinion, since the officer even peeked inside her pencil case. "It's a lucky pencil," she explained. "It's not a weapon." The officer laughed and waved her through, and Julia decided she liked him anyway.

Her friend Harley caught up with them at the gate, because his family was on the same flight, heading to the same island. "Pack gum," he said, jabbing a thumb at his backpack like a wise old traveler. "Last summer on the ferry to the mainland I got so queasy I thought I'd turn inside out. Then my grandpa dragged me up on deck and made me stare at the shoreline the whole way, and it worked. Fixed point, far away. Weird, but it worked."

Julia filed that away, and it turned out to matter, because forty minutes into the flight the plane began bucking through turbulence and her stomach went sour and swimmy. She closed her eyes, which made it worse. Then she remembered Harley on the ferry deck, glued to the shoreline. She leaned to the window and found the horizon, that long steady line where the sea met the sky, and she fixed her eyes on it and refused to let go. Slowly, her stomach settled, like a dog deciding to lie down.

Her mom, in the aisle seat, had gone pale and was clutching the barf bag like a parachute. "Mom," Julia said, "look past me, out the window. Find the horizon. It's fixed, it's far away, and it helps your eyes agree with what your inner ear feels." Her mom leaned across her, stared at the distant line, and breathed out. "Huh," she said. "Better. You're promoted to travel captain." Julia grinned, kept her eyes on the horizon, and said, "First order of business: I'm claiming your pretzels."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: The rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compound interest: divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, so about 12 years at 6 percent.
story:
Brayden spread the bank paperwork across the kitchen table, smoothing the wrinkled flyer with both palms. It advertised a savings account with two options, one paying simple interest and one paying compound interest, both at 6 percent. He had sixty dollars from mowing lawns, and he wanted to know which account would turn it into more money by the time he was seventeen.

"Doing homework?" his dad asked, setting a glass of iced tea on the table. The condensation left a wet ring on the corner of the flyer.

"Kind of," Brayden said. "It's my own money. I want to see what happens over five years." He found a pencil and drew two columns on the back of a cereal box, because that was how his grandfather had taught him to work things out. In a quick flashback, he remembered sitting at this same table two summers ago, when his grandfather had said that messy math on cardboard was the foundation of every good decision. Brayden had rolled his eyes back then. Now he was doing exactly that.

He started with simple interest. Six percent of sixty dollars was three dollars and sixty cents, so every year the bank would add that same amount. Five years meant five times three sixty, which was eighteen dollars. He wrote "78" at the bottom of the first column and circled it.

The compound column was harder. The first year looked the same, three sixty on top of sixty dollars. But the second year, the bank calculated interest on the new total, sixty-three sixty, not just the original sixty. His pencil slowed as he multiplied and carried remainders, and the smell of pencil shavings mixed with the cold sweetness of his dad's tea. The numbers grew, but only a little at a time. He got about eighty dollars and some cents, and he sat back, annoyed. "Two whole dollars difference? That's it?"

He texted Mya, who was the one person he knew who actually liked math. She called him back within a minute. "You only did five years," she said. "The gap gets bigger the longer you wait. Compound keeps building on itself. Simple just repeats."

"So when does it actually get big?" Brayden asked.

Mya was quiet for a second. "There's a thing called the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, and that's about how many years your money takes to double."

Brayden grabbed the pencil. Seventy-two divided by six was twelve. At 6 percent, his money would double in about twelve years. He would be twenty-four. He checked it against his cereal box math, running his simple column out twelve years in his head: sixty plus twelve times three sixty was a bit over one hundred dollars, so simple interest would not quite double his money even in twelve years. Compound would.

He tested it another way, asking himself what would happen at a higher rate, just to see if the rule held its shape. A bigger percentage meant dividing 72 by a bigger number, which meant fewer years to double. That made sense to him, like a hidden pattern that had been there all along, concealed behind the boring small numbers of his five year table. The real problem was not which account was better. It was that five years was too short a window to see the difference clearly.

On Monday he asked Mr. Kerr, his neighbor who used to work at a credit union, whether his math checked out. Mr. Kerr looked over the cereal box, tapping the circled numbers. "The compounding you did is yearly, which is what the flyer means. Your arithmetic is right, and the rule of 72 is a fair estimate." He handed the box back. "Crucial thing you figured out on your own, though. Time does most of the work."

Brayden took the sixty dollars to the bank that afternoon and chose the compound account. It was still only two dollars ahead after five years, and he knew that. But he also knew that at twelve years, when he was twenty-four, the money would double, and he planned to still be saving then.

"Sixty in," the cashier said, stamping the slip. "See you at twenty-four."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government.
story:
Hazel spread the constitution study sheet across the craft table in the community centre art room and frowned at it. On Saturday she had to stand up at the centre's civics showcase and explain one right from the constitution in her own words, and every version she'd tried sounded like she'd copied it straight off the page. Andrew slid into the chair beside her with his notebook.

"Mine's easy," he said. "I just have to say what the Second Amendment covers and why." He tapped her sheet. "Which one are you doing?"

"The First. But every time I try to put it in my own words, I just repeat it." She read aloud. "The First Amendment to the US Constitution protects freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government." She dropped the sheet. "See? I can't get outside it."

Lisa came over from the bulletin board, where she'd been pinning up the showcase schedule. She was the editor of the school paper, the Lincoln Ledger, so Hazel asked her the first thing that came to mind. "Lisa, what protects the press in the United States?"

"Freedom of the press," Lisa said. "It's in the First Amendment, along with religion, speech, peaceful assembly and petitioning the government." She counted them on her fingers. "Five things, one amendment. Why?"

Hazel sat up. That was it. The problem wasn't finding new words, it was seeing the pattern hiding under them. Five freedoms bundled together, and each one was a way people got to say or believe or ask something without the government stopping them. She could test that idea. She grabbed a paper plate from the craft shelf and drew five spokes around the edge, one for each freedom, and wrote "the First Amendment" in the middle. It was only a prototype, but it made the shape visible.

Mr. Huang, who ran the centre and was stacking chairs by the window, wandered over to look. "That's a nice objective way to show it," he said. "Can I borrow that idea for the display table?" He offered Hazel a marker from the supply cupboard and, without being asked, brought over a second chair so Andrew would have somewhere to sit while he worked.

Hazel had been planning to conquer her nerves by memorizing the amendment word for word, but now she changed her mind about that. Instead she would hold up the plate and say, in her own words, that the First Amendment protects five freedoms that all come down to the same thing: people can believe, speak, publish, gather and ask. Andrew copied the plate design into his notebook and said he wished his topic had a shape like that.

At the showcase on Saturday, Hazel stood in front of the folding table with her plate propped on a stack of books. "Pick a spoke," she told the first kid who stopped, "and I'll tell you what it means in plain words."

The kid pointed to the top spoke and Hazel grinned. "Religion. Okay, here goes."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
Lauren stood in front of the mirror in her bedroom, doing the grapevine step for the fourteenth time. Left foot to the side, right foot behind, left foot to the side, tap. On the fourteenth attempt, her right foot caught her left ankle and she sat down hard on the rug.

"Stupid feet," she told them, but her feet implied nothing back.

The dance was tomorrow night, her first one, and there was a real problem: she could slow dance fine, but the whole grade knew that Kason had no partner, and if he stood against the gym wall all night looking like a lost sock, she would feel terrible. Also, she wanted to dance with him, which was a separate and more embarrassing problem.

She flopped onto her bed and thought about last summer, when her grandmother had dragged her to a community picnic. Lauren had expected bingo and casseroles, but instead a speaker crackled and forty people, most of them old enough to be descendants of the pioneers who had built the town hall, turned to face the same direction and started moving together. No partners. Just rows of people doing the same set of steps, over and over, like one enormous friendly machine. Lauren had hidden behind the lemonade table, but she remembered the shape of it: grapevine, tap, turn, clap.

She sat straight up. They had all been facing the same direction. Nobody needed anybody's hand. She could learn six steps and so could Kason, and then they would be dancing together, technically, without her having to ask him anything.

She grabbed her phone and called Emma-Rose. "What songs do you think they'll play?"

"Ms. Munro promised a line dance at least twice," Emma-Rose said. "That's what she called it, a line dance. Everybody repeats the same steps facing the same direction, like a herd of very happy cows."

Lauren laughed so hard she had to put the phone on the bed. "That's the thing from the picnic. Okay, practice plan. My house, now, kitchen floor, socks."

When Emma-Rose arrived, they pushed the kitchen table against the fridge and marked a line on the floor with painter's tape. "Face the window," Lauren instructed. "Same direction, both of us, always." They grapevined into the counter, tapped the refrigerator, and clipped the tape line with their toes, but by the sixth run they stopped crashing and started grinning.

The next evening, the gym smelled like floor wax and nervousness. When the DJ called the line dance, Kason drifted toward the wall, and Lauren marched over. "You only need six steps," she said. "Face the window with me."

He frowned. "What if I'm terrible?"

"Then you'll be terrible in a line of thirty kids instead of alone by the punch bowl." She held out her arm like a tour guide. Kason sighed, stepped in beside her, and on the first grapevine he bumped her elbow, but on the second one he didn't, and by the clap he was laughing.

"You planned this," he said.

Lauren faced the window and tapped. "Maybe check your feet before you accuse people."

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: When a variable appears on both sides, as in 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, subtracting 3x from both sides gathers the variable on one side: 2x + 2 = 10.
story:
Xavier signed the library contract at the front desk, promising to keep the study room quiet, and Ms. MacLeod handed him the key. It was a privilege, she said, only two seventh graders had it. He carried his math worksheet to the back table, where Gabriella already had her pencil out and Hashim was balancing a book on his head until she glared at him.

The problem was 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, and both sides had an x on them. Xavier stared at it. Which x was he supposed to move? If he picked wrong, the whole thing might collapse. He decided to subtract 3x from both sides, wrote carefully, and got 2x + 2 = 10. That looked possible. Gabriella leaned over and frowned at his page.

"You did it wrong," she said. "You're supposed to take the 5x away, because it's first." She erased her own work, subtracted 5x from both sides, and ended up with 2 = negative 2x + 10. Her pencil hovered. "Wait. Mine still has an x with a negative on it. That can't be right."

Before Xavier could answer, a folded note slid across the table. Hashim had written it while they argued: "You both got 4. Check." Gabriella narrowed her eyes, worked down her own page, subtracted 10 from both sides, then divided, and there it was: 4. Xavier solved his, and 2x + 2 = 10 came out to 4 as well. Two distinct roads, same answer, and neither one had fallen apart.

Gabriella put her pencil down slowly. "So it works either way," she said. "I changed my mind. You can move whichever x you want, as long as you do it to both sides." She tapped the negative sign in her work. "Even if it looks strange halfway through." Hashim took the book off his head and wrote one more note, sliding it over like a spy passing secrets: "Can we contract to never argue about math again." Xavier laughed and signed it, then Gabriella signed it, each name going under the last one like a real agreement.

Ms. MacLeod appeared at the door of the study room. "Everything all right back here?" she asked.

Xavier slid the signed note across the table toward her. "We just made a treaty," he said.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Nervousness triggers the release of adrenaline, which speeds up the heart and pulls blood away from the stomach, causing the "butterflies" feeling.
story:
The gym doors were still two hallways away, and Koen already looked like he was going to be sick. Maeva stopped beside the trophy case and studied him. His face was pale, his hand pressed flat against his stomach.

"I can't do it," he said. "My heart's going crazy and my stomach feels like it's full of moths. Before we even got inside."

Maeva had been noticing her own stomach doing a slow, gradual flip ever since the car ride, so she wanted to know what was going on. "My cousin calls those butterflies," she said. "She says when you're nervous, your body lets out adrenaline. It speeds up your heart and pulls blood away from your stomach. That's why it flips."

Koen blinked at her. "Butterflies. Huh. So everybody in there has that?"

That was the question, wasn't it? Maeva looked down the hallway at the decorated doors, the streamers, the kids hovering near the water fountain pretending they weren't hovering. She couldn't see inside anyone's stomach. But if nervousness did this to Koen out here, she could make an inference: probably half the kids by the fountain had racing hearts too, they were just hiding it better.

"I have an idea," she said. "Let's test it. If it's just adrenaline, then moving around should help, like it's fuel. Run to the end of the hall and back."

"You want me to run?"

"Science, Koen."

He sighed and ran, sneakers squeaking, past a startled Ms. Weber carrying a box of cups. He came back breathing hard but grinning. "Weird. The stomach thing is still there, but it feels less like doom now."

Before they went in, Maeva checked her phone. Nellie had texted from inside: "PSA for anyone in the hallway: the punch table has no line because everyone's too scared to be first. Also my heart is beating so loud I can hear it. Is that normal??"

Maeva typed back: "Totally normal. It's adrenaline. It speeds up your heart and pulls blood away from your stomach, so you get the flip feeling. Nervousness does it to everybody. Koen and I ran it off. Half the gym probably has butterflies too, they're just better actors than us."

Nellie replied with a single line of exclamation points.

Maeva put the phone away. Maybe nervous stomachs were something you inherited, like her mom's habit of pacing before every party, and you couldn't stop the butterflies from showing up. But you could decide what to do once they landed.

She took Koen's sleeve. "Come on. We're going to be first in the punch line so nobody else has to be."

"Okay," he said, and pushed open the gym doors.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
story:
Camille spread her survey results across the library table like a card dealer. Fifty students, and the pattern jumped out: kids who ate breakfast mostly had higher grades. Her poster was due Friday, and the title she had written in green marker said "Breakfast Makes You Smarter." Teagan slid into the chair across from her and read it upside down.

"That's not right," Teagan said. "My cousin eats breakfast every day and she's failing math."

"One person doesn't break a pattern," Camille said, but the words felt wobbly. She flipped her pencil between her fingers. Abbas arrived carrying three books about the brain, dumped them next to her papers, and started to dismantle her neat stacks to build the books into a tower instead. "Stop," she said, then stopped herself. "Wait. Abbas, do you eat breakfast?"

"Every day," Abbas said. "My mother makes it before school. She came here as a refugee, and she says she will never send us out hungry." He shrugged. "But my grades went up this year, and last year I ate breakfast too."

Camille tapped her pencil against the table, hearing the tiny wooden clicks. Something was circling in her head, a question she couldn't see directly. She wrote it at the top of a fresh page: what if breakfast wasn't the cause at all? What if something else made both things happen? She looked at her survey again, hunting for a question she had asked but never used: "Who wakes you up in the morning?" The breakfast kids mostly had a parent or grandparent at home, making food, checking homework, setting a bedtime. The no-breakfast kids mostly got themselves up.

She tested it. Kids with an adult at home in the morning had higher grades whether they ate breakfast or not. Two kids in her class who ate breakfast alone, cold cereal in a dark kitchen, had average grades. Her pattern was really about mornings with adults in them, and breakfast just came along for the ride.

"Two things happening together doesn't prove one causes the other," she told Teagan, arranging the numbers into two new columns. "Something else can cause both."

"There's a word for that," Teagan said, flipping through one of Abbas's books. "Correlation."

Mr. Holloway passed by with a cart of returns and paused at her table. "Found your answer, or found a better question?"

"A better question," Camille said, and she turned the poster over to its blank side. She uncapped the green marker and started again, printing slowly: "Breakfast and Grades: Together, But Why?" Abbas placed the last book on top of his tower, and it stood, wobbling, in the lamplight.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: A crescendo means gradually getting louder, and a diminuendo or decrescendo means gradually getting softer.
story:
Mason set his keyboard on the workbench between the snow shovel and a box of nails, because the garage was the only place his mom let him practice loud. Caius dragged his amp in through the side door and dropped his drum sticks on the cement.

"Saturday's the talent show," Caius said. "Ms. Wanjiru only picked us because nobody else signed up. If we sound like a car crash, she'll wish she hadn't." He wanted the act to work more than Mason did, and he kept saying so.

They ran the piece from the top. It started soft, which Mason liked, and halfway through his sheet music showed a word in fancy italics: crescendo. He had never practiced the song all the way through with Caius before, and when they hit that bar, Caius suddenly slammed the drums at full blast. Mason flinched so hard he knocked a paint can off the bench, and it landed with a clang that made them both freeze.

"What was that?" Mason asked, picking up the can.

"That's the loud part," Caius said. "It says crescendo."

Mason looked at the page. The crescendo stretched across eight whole bars, not one. He tapped the dynamic marking at the start and the one at the end. "It can't mean jump straight to loud," he said. "Then why would it go on for so long? It has to mean you get there a little at a time."

"So what, I just guess how fast to get louder?"

"Let's test it," Mason said. "Play your quiet groove and add a tiny bit every two bars. I'll follow you." He had been thinking about how a song could feel like it was climbing without the listener knowing exactly when the climb started, and this seemed like a way to hear it.

They tried it. Mason crept the keyboard volume up alongside Caius, bar by bar, and by the last crash the garage door buzzed faintly with the sound. It was the first time the song had given him chills instead of making him feel humiliated in front of his best friend. Later in the piece the music marked a diminuendo, and they tested that too, getting softer gradually instead of cutting off, until the ending faded out like a radio drifting down a highway.

Brooke came over after dinner with her trumpet case and a concussion story from gym class that made Caius laugh so hard he fell off the amp. She asked if their plan for the dynamics was feasible, since trumpet was not great at whispering. They tried it anyway, and on the first run Brooke followed Mason down the diminuendo so smoothly that Caius pointed his stick at her like a conductor.

"Again," Caius said, counting them in. "From the top, and this time nobody drops the paint can."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta.
story:
Jaxson set the onion on the cutting board and stared at it the way his sister stared at math homework. His mom had texted that she'd be home at eight, tired and hungry, and he wanted dinner waiting for her for once. On the kitchen tablet, Aminata waved from her own kitchen two streets over.

"Remember the claw," she said. "Curl your fingertips under, so only your knuckles face the knife. That way the blade can't expose your fingers, just the onion."

Jaxson curled his fingers like a bear paw and pressed down. The first cut squished sideways and the onion rolled, but the second landed clean, and after that the slices came off the board in half-moons, thinner each time. His eyes burned so badly he had to chop the last part with his head tipped back, which made Aminata laugh so hard she dropped her own knife on her counter with a clang.

The sauce came next. Canned tomatoes, a splash of oil, the onion, a pinch of salt. While it simmered, he dropped pasta into a big pot, and when the water boiled the surface spun in a tight whirl, like a tiny turbine pulling everything toward the middle. He fished out a noodle at nine minutes, bit it, and called it done.

He carried the pot to the sink and tipped it to pour.

"Wait!" Aminata's voice shot out of the tablet so loud the speaker crackled. "Save a cup of the water first. Pasta releases starch into its cooking water, and a splash of that starchy water helps a sauce thicken and cling to the pasta."

Jaxson stopped with the pot halfway over the drain. "It's just dirty water," he said.

"It looks like dirty water. Just save a cup and try it. If I'm wrong, you can pour the whole rest down the drain and tell me I ruined your sauce."

He set the pot down, ladled a mugful of the cloudy water, and set it by the stove. Then he looked hard at his sauce. It was thin and pale, and honestly it looked a bit impoverished, like something from a cafeteria tray. He had been planning to pretend it was rustic. He stirred in a splash of the starchy water and watched.

Nothing dramatic happened at first. Then, as he kept stirring, the sauce stopped sitting in a puddle under the spoon and started riding on it. He added another splash, and the tomatoes turned glossy, clinging to the spoon the way syrup clings. He tasted it and stood very still for a second.

"Okay," he said slowly. "You were right. It's actually sticking to everything."

"Told you. Now mix the pasta in, don't just pour sauce on top."

He tipped the drained pasta into the pan and folded it through with the wooden spoon. Every noodle came out coated. At five to eight, he heard the front door, and his mom came into the kitchen still wearing her work badge. She looked at the pan, then at him, then at the mug of cloudy water sitting by the stove.

"What's that?" she asked.

"That," Jaxson said, lifting the pan onto the table, "is the secret ingredient."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas.
story:
Victoria stood in the cleaning aisle of Martino's Grocery with her dad's list in her hand: laundry detergent, stain remover, and something for the mildew on the shower curtain. Her mother had left that morning for a two-week nursing assignment, and Victoria had volunteered to take over the laundry. She wanted to prove she could handle the whole job, sorting to folding, without a single text home for help.

She reached for the chlorine bleach first, because the mildew line was underlined twice. Then she grabbed a bottle of tub cleaner with a spray trigger. It was only when she turned the tub cleaner around to check the price that she saw the warning on the back, printed small under the directions: contains ammonia. Do not mix with chlorine bleach.

The words nudged something loose in her memory. In October, in Mr. Barrett's science room, he had been mixing solutions at the front bench while the class copied a diagram of lichen off the board. A kid named Aarya had asked why he kept the bottles so far apart, and Mr. Barrett had said, "Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia, because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas." Then he had made them document the rule in their lab notebooks before anyone touched a chemical. Victoria had written it, drawn a box around it, and forgotten it until now.

She held both bottles up and read the labels again, side by side. The bleach said nothing about ammonia, and the ammonia cleaner said nothing about bleach, but each one named the other as the danger. So the rule worked from both directions, like an obstinate door that only opened if you pushed the correct side. At home, her dad kept the bleach on the shelf above the washer. If she sprayed the tub cleaner in the same small bathroom while a bleach-soaked curtain sat in the tub, would that count as mixing? She put the tub cleaner back on the shelf and chose a bottle labeled "bleach-free" instead, then tested her reasoning once more by walking the whole aisle and reading every mildew product. Not one combined the two.

At the register, Alexandria from her geometry class was bagging groceries. "Two cleaners and detergent?" Alexandria said. "Big cleaning day?"

"Laundry week," Victoria said. "My mom's away."

When Victoria got home, she sorted the laundry into three piles on her bedroom floor, whites, darks, and the red towel that had turned her father's socks pink last summer. She carried the whites down to the basement and stopped on the last step. The bleach was on the shelf above the washer, right where she'd expected. Beside it, unlabeled, sat a half-gallon jug of cloudy liquid that had not been there that morning. Her dad called down the stairs, "Found ammonia for the tub, sweetheart. It was on sale." Victoria set her basket down and carried the jug straight back up to the kitchen cabinet, far from the basement shelf, before she started the machine.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: You may never divide both sides of an equation by zero, because division by zero has no answer.
story:
Emily sat at the kitchen table with her math book open to a page of equations, a pencil, and a bag of pretzels she was not technically supposed to have before dinner. Somewhere in her science folder there was also a worksheet asking her to classify a list of animals, and the wolf had taken her a whole two seconds: carnivore, obviously. The equations were less cooperative. "x plus seven equals twelve" was fine, but the book kept sliding toward things like "three x minus five equals sixteen," and her pencil kept hovering instead of moving.

Aariz arrived through the back door without knocking, holding a folded paper like it was a winning lottery ticket. His want was simple and he announced it before sitting down: he was going to win Friday's math club challenge, and the prize was a Mr. Koné-approved "Grand Thinker" pencil, and Sebastian had won the last one, so this was personal. He slapped the paper on the table between the pretzels and her book. "Prepare to witness one equal two."

"Impossible," Emily said.

"That's the beauty of it. Watch." He wrote out his steps, narrating each move like a magician. Start with a equals b. Multiply both sides by a. Subtract b squared from both sides. Factor. Then he divided both sides by a minus b, and both sides came out identical, and there it was: one equals two. He leaned back. "Mr. Koné won't be able to tear this apart. I've checked it four times."

Emily had learned one real thing that week, which was that an equation was like a seesaw: whatever you did to one side, you had to do to the other, or the whole thing tipped over. She copied Aariz's steps onto her own paper, slow and suspicious, the way she checked the latch on the hamster cage twice. The steps held up. Multiply both sides, fine. Subtract from both sides, fine. Then she hit the division, and instead of moving past it she did something Aariz hadn't thought to do. She went back to the very first line and tried numbers. If a equals b, then she could pick a equals three and b equals three. Which meant a minus b was three minus three. She wrote it down and stared at it. "Aariz. What's anything divided by zero?"

Aariz looked at her, then at his beautiful proof, then at her paper. His shoulders dropped about an inch. "It has no answer," he said, mostly to the pretzel bag. "You can never divide both sides by zero. That's where it's hiding." It was, Emily thought, almost ironic: the sneakiest move in his proof was the one step that looked the most ordinary, a plain little division sitting there in the middle of everything.

"You could still present it," she offered. "Show the trick, then catch it. Mr. Koné likes catching things."

Aariz sat up straight again and began folding the paper into a paper airplane. "New plan. I beat Sebastian by finding the trap before he does." He aimed it at her science folder, where the wolf waited to be classified.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: A thesis can preview the argument by naming its supporting points in the same order the body paragraphs will discuss them.
story:
Bentley stared at the blank document on the family laptop like it had insulted his grandmother. The assignment was due Monday, and Mr. Eze had been very clear: thesis statement first, then an outline with three points, then the actual essay. "Nobody drafts before the outline," he had said, waving a marker like a sword. Bentley had drafts. Three of them. All terrible. His argument about why the school should keep recess was deteriorating badly, and it was starting to feel personal.

He flopped onto the kitchen stool and pulled out his phone. He texted Idris, who had finished his essay on Wednesday like some kind of wizard.

Bentley: help. my essay is a disaster sandwich
Idris: what's on the sandwich
Bentley: two slices of nothing and a filling of panic
Idris: lol. did you do the outline? the three points thing?
Bentley: outlines are for cowards
Idris: outlines are for people who finish

Bentley put the phone down and glared at his notes. He had three reasons to keep recess: it helped kids focus, it made school less miserable, and it let kids make friends. Fine. He typed a thesis: "The school should keep recess because it helps kids focus, makes school less miserable, and lets kids make friends." It felt weirdly good, like a door clicking shut.

He drafted fast after that, paragraph by paragraph, one for each reason. Then, reading it over, he decided his friendship paragraph was his strongest, so he moved it to the top. Then he moved the focus paragraph to the middle, because the middle was the weakest spot, and everyone knew that. He sat back, pleased. Then sat forward again, frowning. He scrolled up to his thesis. It listed focus first, then misery, then friendship. His paragraphs now went friendship, focus, misery. The two lists didn't match. His thesis had promised readers one order and delivered another, like a menu that brings your dessert first and your burger last.

He tested it out loud, in a robot voice, because that helped him think. "Reason one: it lets kids make friends." He looked at paragraph one. Friends. "Reason two: it helps kids focus." Paragraph two. Focus. "Reason three: less miserable." Paragraph three. Miserable. If he just rewrote the thesis so the points appeared in the new order, everything lined up. The thesis could preview the whole argument, point by point, in the same order the paragraphs would discuss them. He grinned. His essay wasn't a disaster sandwich anymore. It was a neat, intricate little machine.

He texted Idris one more time.

Bentley: update. the sandwich is now a lasagna. layered. structured. beautiful
Idris: did you finally write the outline
Bentley: technically the outline wrote me

Leon peeked in from the hallway, holding a bag of chips. "Who are you texting at nine at night?"

"My academic rival," Bentley said. "Get out of my office. I'm finalizing a masterpiece."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A pill organizer has a compartment for each day of the week, so an empty compartment shows that day's dose has already been taken.
story:
The train from the north arrived at platform four at exactly 4:15, and Kate squeezed past a man with a suitcase to get close to the doors. Her grandfather was coming to stay for a whole week, the longest visit ever, and she had promised her mom she would not lose him in the crowd. When the doors hissed open, he stepped out holding a small canvas bag in one hand and a plastic box in the other, the box with seven little lids along the top.

"There she is," he said. "Kate the Great, master of the train station." He let her carry the canvas bag but kept the plastic box in his own hand, and on the walk to the car he mentioned, almost to himself, that the old dining car on this line had gone extinct years ago, along with half the routes. He talked about trains the whole way home, and Kate mostly listened, because that was what the visit was for.

The trouble started on the second morning. Kate came downstairs for cereal and found her grandfather standing at the counter, holding the plastic box up to the window, turning it over. "I can't recall whether I took my morning pills," he said. "I stood right here, and now I can't recall."

Kate was about to say take them anyway, but something stopped her. "Wait," she said. "What is that box, exactly?"

"It's a pill organizer," he said. "One compartment for each day of the week. I fill it up Sundays."

Kate leaned in. Seven lids, labeled S, M, T, W, T, F, S. She lifted Tuesday's lid and found it empty. She lifted Monday's, and it was empty too. "Then you took them," she said slowly, working it out as she spoke. "If Tuesday's compartment is empty, that dose is already gone. You took Tuesday morning, or someone did."

"I filled it Sunday night, I know that much," her grandfather said. He still looked doubtful, so Kate made a test of it. "Don't take anything yet," she said. "Watch." She opened Wednesday's compartment, which was full, then Tuesday's, which was not, then Wednesday's again. "If you forget tomorrow, we check Thursday. Full means take them, empty means done." His shoulders came down from around his ears.

He did forget the next morning, and the morning after that, and Kate began to wonder if his memory problem was worse than anyone had said. She persisted anyway, checking the box with him every day, marking a little check on the kitchen calendar each time. By Friday he was checking it himself, holding it up to the light and saying "full" or "empty" out loud like a code word between them. When her friend Drew came over Saturday, he guessed the visit was going badly because he was biased toward expecting disasters from Drew-grade evidence, which was one blurry rumor from his cousin. Kate just laughed and showed him the box. "It's a system," she said. On Sunday night, her grandfather sat at the counter with the bottles lined up, snapping new pills into each compartment, one day at a time. He tapped Tuesday's lid shut and slid the box across the counter toward her. "Your turn to check me next week," he said.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The climax is the turning point of a story, the moment of highest tension when the main conflict is decided one way or the other.
story:
Kate's story was due on Friday, and by Wednesday she still could not get the dialogue right. Every time a character spoke, she piled the words together in one long block with no punctuation, and Ms. Francis had written "Who is talking here?" in the margin three times. Kate sat in the library at lunch with her draft spread out, chewing the end of her pencil.

Charles-Antoine dropped his backpack on the table across from her. "Is that the story about the haunted gym?" he asked. He wanted to be first in the class to read his aloud, and he had already finished his, so he had time to bother other people.

"It's not haunted," Kate said. "It's about a kid who finds a door behind the bleachers, and she hears something behind it." She turned the page toward him. "But Ms. Francis says I have to punctuate the dialogue and cut half of it, and she circled something at the end and wrote 'Is this your climax?'"

"Mine has a shark," Charles-Antoine said. He read her last page anyway, because he read everything. "The part at the end, when your main character just walks home, that can't be the climax. Nothing gets decided. It's the most boring part of the whole story."

August slid into the next chair with a sandwich and no permission to join. "I read it over her shoulder in homeroom," he said. "The best part is when she puts her ear against the door. That's obviously the climax."

Charles-Antoine shook his head. "The climax is the shark attack. In every story."

"You don't have a shark in every story," August said. "Use your brain."

Kate pulled the draft back and read her own pages. August was arguing for the door scene, Charles-Antoine for the ending, and she had a third idea forming. She took a clean sheet and wrote the three scenes from her story in order: the door, the ending, and the part she had not mentioned, where her main character finally opens the door and whatever is inside either gets out or does not. She circled the third one. "The climax is the turning point," she said. "It's the moment of highest tension, when the main conflict gets decided one way or the other. My conflict is whether she opens the door. It gets decided right there. The door-listening is just buildup, and walking home is what happens after."

August frowned at her circled scene. "So the part I liked isn't even the important one."

"It's important," Kate said. "It just isn't where things turn." She looked at her draft and saw the other problem at once. Her last two pages were about the main character walking home and eating dinner, and now she knew why Ms. Francis had circled them. She cut them. "I need a new ending. Short."

Charles-Antoine leaned over her shoulder while she rewrote the door scene with real punctuation, each speaker on a new line, commas before the quotation marks. "Read it out loud," he said. She did, and heard where the pauses went, and fixed two more commas. In the new ending, her main character opened the door, found the old team mascot costume that had been missing for six years, and laughed until the sound filled the whole gym.

On Friday, Ms. Francis read Kate's story to the class, and Charles-Antoine did not get to go first. Afterward he raised his hand. "Her story was infectious," he said. "Now I want to rewrite mine without the shark."

"Your shark got a concussion from hitting the boat," August said. "Just let him recover and cut the rest."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In most major sports, home teams win more than half their games, an effect called home advantage.
story:
The scoreboard glowed 2 to 1 for the Falcons as the second-period buzzer sounded, and Kaitlyn scrambled over three rows of coats to reach Quinten and Emery before intermission ended. "Eighteen minutes," Emery said, pointing at the clock above the ice. "If we want to prove it to Mr. Aydın before the third period starts, we'd better hurry."

The argument had begun on the drive over, when their dad mentioned that Mr. Aydın, who ran the rink's snack bar, had laughed and said the Falcons only looked good because they were playing at home. Quinten had shrugged like it was obvious. "Teams just play better at home," he said. Emery disagreed. "That's superstition. A rink is a rink."

Kaitlyn wasn't sure, and not knowing bugged her. Between bites of nachos, she pulled out her phone and started checking standings for the major leagues, hockey, basketball, baseball, football. "Look at this," she said, shoving the screen toward Emery. "Every one of these. Home teams win more than half their games. Not sometimes. More than half, every season, in basically every major sport."

"So what do they call it?" Emery asked. "Home magic?"

"It's called home advantage," Kaitlyn said. "It's a real thing."

Quinten did a drumroll on the snack bar counter. "So we win tonight because of our crowd, and we'd lose anywhere else. Ha."

But Kaitlyn had gone quiet, scrolling deeper. "Quinten," she said slowly, "where does Mr. Aydın's team play?" They checked the schedule, and there it was: the Falcons' regular rink had closed for repairs last month. Tonight's game, the one everyone had been calling a home game all season out of habit, was actually at this rink, forty minutes from their own town, with mostly the other team's fans in the stands.

"Then we can test it," Emery said. "If home advantage is the whole story, the Falcons should lose. Right now."

They carried the nachos down to the glass just as the puck dropped. The Falcons were outshot twice in the first five minutes, and Quinten groaned, "See? Home advantage," but then the Falcons' winger stole the puck, raced up the ice alone, and buried it. The goal light spun red, and Mr. Aydín, wiping his hands on his apron, called over the crowd, "Okay, okay. Maybe your team's just good."

"Maybe it's both," Kaitlyn said, grinning as the horn blasted. "Now we have ten minutes to figure out how good."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false, while an opinion expresses a belief, feeling or judgment that evidence cannot prove.
story:
The timer on the microwave said 11:42, which meant Hazel and Spencer had exactly eighteen minutes to find his missing controller before his little brother got home from swimming and turned the living room upside down. Spencer was already doing that, in fact, sweeping couch cushions onto the floor with the energy of a search-and-rescue team.

"It was Jan," Spencer said, arms full of cushions. "Jan lost it. He had it last."

Hazel paused. "Had it last, or lost it?"

"Same thing."

"It's really not." She held up a hand before he could argue. "If you say Jan took it home on Friday, that's a claim we can check. We text him, he looks in his backpack, done. True or false. But if you say Jan is careless and loses everything, that's an opinion. Nobody can prove it. It's just what you believe."

Spencer dropped the cushions. "Fine. That's your opinion of my opinion."

"That's a fact about your opinion," Hazel said, and he actually cracked a smile.

They texted Jan, and while they waited, Hazel kept looking. She wasn't ready to delegate the whole search to Jan's memory, because Jan once forgot his own birthday. The room told a story if you read it in order: a popcorn bowl on its side, a blanket dragged toward the hallway, and, on the bookshelf, a suspicious gap between Spencer's dictionary and his volcano book. The books were stacked in a neat column, except one spot where something square and dark had been wedged in sideways.

"Spencer," she said slowly, not pointing yet, because if she was wrong she wanted to be wrong quietly. "What's behind the volcano book?"

He crossed the room, pulled the book forward, and there it was, the controller, jammed vertically into the shelf like a secret. The little brother had done it. That was the only answer that fit, because the little brother liked to hide things and then sit back and watch everyone panic, which Hazel considered genuinely reckless when the thing being hidden was the controller for a game night scheduled for tonight at noon.

The phone buzzed. Jan had replied with a photo of his backpack, empty except for a sandwich, and one line: "Why are you asking me, weirdos?"

Spencer stood there holding the controller, ears going pink. "So my claim was false," he said. "And I said it like it was a fact."

"It happens to everyone," Hazel said, putting the cushion stack back so the room looked normal. "My mom says our family can't reach consensus on anything, and now I get why. Half our arguments are facts nobody checks and opinions nobody labels."

The garage door rattled. Swimming bag, dripping goggles, and a little brother strolling in with a suspiciously innocent face.

"Hey," Spencer said, holding up the controller. "Bookshelf. Nice try."

The little brother's eyes went wide, then he grinned and said, "Took you long enough."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true.
story:
Ellie sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with the remote in her hand, waiting for Hillary and Mahi to arrive. Her homework sheet lay on the coffee table: find five persuasion tricks in real ads and explain why they work. She had recorded an hour of shows the night before, and now she planned to hunt through them like a detective.

When Hillary and Mahi flopped onto the couch, Ellie pressed play. The first commercial blared out that a sneaker was "the choice of champions everywhere." Ellie scribbled the words down. "That's a bandwagon appeal," she said. "Everybody's buying it, so you should too." Mahi nodded, but then she frowned. "That one star athlete in the next ad, though. He's a celebrity testimonial. He gets paid to say the shoes made him fast." Hillary snorted. "He was fast before the shoes. He'd be fast in shower sandals." Ellie laughed and wrote that down too.

They kept going. A cereal ad called a rival brand "soggy cardboard," and Ellie underlined the loaded words twice. A face cream promised skin like "morning vapor," soft and glowing, which made Hillary ask, "Is vapor even a good thing to put on your face?" Nobody had an answer, but Ellie added it to her list anyway, because noticing weirdness counted.

Then Mahi leaned forward. "There's this thing at school. People say the cafeteria ladies water down the juice to save money. I believed it, and I was trying to figure out why today." She paused. "Then I counted. I've heard it five times this week. Five. From different people, but every single one of them heard it from the same person, Marco." Ellie set down her pencil. "Wait. Do you believe it because of proof, or because you've heard it so many times?" Mahi shrugged. "That's the thing. There's no proof. It just feels true."

Ellie's older sister had a psychology book on the shelf, and Ellie pulled it down and flipped pages while the others watched. "Here," she said, running her finger under a paragraph. "In a 1977 study, Lynn Hasher and colleagues found that people rated statements as more likely to be true after seeing them repeated, whether or not they were true." Hillary read it over her shoulder. "So repetition alone does it. Not evidence. Just hearing it again and again." Ellie chewed her pencil. Was that why ads ran a hundred times, why Marco kept repeating the juice story? She wanted to test it.

So they tried an experiment right there in the living room. Ellie invented a fake fact, that the school fountain water turned your shoelaces slightly blue, and said it out loud once. Nobody bought it. Then she said it again at breakfast, and again at lunch, and by the end of the week she said it a fifth time, and a kid in science class told her, "Yeah, everyone knows about the shoelace thing." Ellie grinned and wrote her whole project that night, but first she went back to the cafeteria line and asked for the juice.

She took a sip, looked straight at Marco, and said, "Tastes full strength to me. Got proof?"
