story:
At dinner Harper pushed her rice around the plate and waited for a gap in the conversation. Her little brother was telling their dad everything about a video game nobody else cared about, which gave her time to rehearse the words in her head. She had spent the whole bus ride home replaying what had happened in the gym hallway, and now the sentence she needed kept changing shape, like it didn't want to be said out loud.

"Adrianna's not talking to me," she finally said. The clink of forks went quiet.

Her mom set down the water glass. "Since when? This morning you were fine."

"Since lunch. She grabbed my phone out of my hands and started reading my texts, and I told her to stop. I said I don't want anyone reading my stuff without asking, not even her." Harper kept her eyes on her plate, but she could feel both parents looking at her. "So now she says I'm being dramatic."

"Are you?" her dad asked, not in a mean way, in the real-question way.

That was the thing Harper had been turning over all afternoon. She didn't think she was being dramatic. Her stomach had been tight since fifth period, that jittery kind of tight, the kind Ms. Jung had once called anxiety when she noticed Harper couldn't sit still during a fire drill. But she had also wondered, more than once, whether the tight feeling meant she was wrong. Maybe a small thing had grown big only because she'd made it big.

"It's a boundary," Harper said. "That's what it's called. A limit about what you're comfortable with, like how people treat you or use your stuff." She'd learned the word last month, when Lennon had calmly told a boy in science class to stop borrowing her calculator, and Lennon hadn't seemed dramatic at all. She'd seemed like someone who knew where her lines were.

Her mom tilted her head. "And did you set it calmly, or did you yell?"

"I said please first," Harper said. "Then I said it without the please."

Her dad laughed into his napkin. Her mom didn't, but her shoulders softened a little. "Tomorrow, why don't you try something," she said. "Same words, but say them like they're already settled, not like you're asking permission for them."

Harper thought about that while she cleared the table. The coping ritual she usually relied on, ten slow breaths with her eyes closed, had gotten her through the afternoon, but breathing hadn't fixed anything. The problem was still sitting out there, cold and barren, waiting for her at school.

At lunch the next day she found Adrianna alone at the end of the long table, hood up, tray untouched. Harper sat down across from her instead of beside her, which felt deliberate in a way she liked. "I'm not sorry for what I said," she told her. "But I am sorry I grabbed the phone back so hard. That part I could've done better."

Adrianna's hood came down halfway. "You really don't want me reading your texts?"

"Not without asking. You can ask anytime."

Adrianna picked up her fork and stabbed a piece of chicken. "Okay. Ask first. Fine."

"Fine," Harper said, and stole a fry off the tray.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Detergent molecules have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water.
story:
Samantha pressed her nose against the glass of the community room at the bank while her mother stood in line to deposit the family savings jar. It was Customer Appreciation Day, and Ms. Charles, the teller who always wore a pin shaped like a pig, had set out pizza for the school savings club. Samantha, Alayna, and Korbin had each earned a slice for hitting their deposit goals. Then Korbin told a joke about a piggy bank with a tail, Samantha laughed with a full mouth, and a dab of orange grease dropped straight onto the front of her white hoodie. Picture day was Thursday.

"That's the special savings club hoodie," Alayna said, sounding as worried as Samantha felt. "Ms. Charles said we have to wear it for the group photo."

At home, Samantha ran the spot under the tap and scrubbed. The stain stayed, shiny and stubborn, like it had decided to move in. Her mother, who was frugal about almost everything, had already declared that replacing the hoodie was out of the question. "You're eleven," she said. "Time you learned to do a load yourself. Sorting, washing, folding. I'll be at the bank until six."

Samanther stared at the detergent bottle, then at the stain, and thought about the problem the way Ms. Charles thought about a miscounted drawer: something hidden was going on. Water alone had done nothing, which meant grease and water were not simply mixing. She folded a paper towel, dotted one corner with cooking oil, and dipped half of it in plain water. The oil stayed put. Then she rubbed a drop of detergent onto the other half and dipped it again. The oil lifted away and clouded the water like smoke. She tried it once more with cold water instead of warm, just to be sure, and the same thing happened.

"It's like the detergent has two ends," she told Alayna on the phone that night. "One end grabs the water and one end grabs the grease, so it lifts the greasy stuff off and carries it into the wash water. That's why my tap scrubbing did nothing. There was nothing to grab both sides."

"You sound like a scientist," Alayna said. "Can I come over? My gym shirt has a mystery smell and my mom says if I ruin one more load she'll make me hand-wash everything forever."

The next afternoon, Alayna arrived with her shirt, and Korbin showed up too, claiming he only wanted to watch but bringing his own soccer socks in a plastic bag. Samantha ran the operation like Ms. Charles ran the teller line. She sorted everything into piles, whites and darks, checked pockets, and explained that Alayna's red gym shorts had to stay out of the white load unless she wanted pink socks. Korbin offered to help by jamming everything into one machine, but Samantha refused to comply with that plan. The old washer groaned through its cycle while the drain hose coiled behind it like an intestine, and the three of them sat on the laundry room floor playing cards until the spin cycle rattled the detergent bottle on the shelf.

When Samantha pulled the hoodie from the dryer, the stain was gone. Alayna's shirt smelled like clean cotton instead of mystery, and Korbin's socks had come out merely gray instead of toxic. They folded everything on the dining table, Samantha showing the others her mother's trick of matching sock pairs before anything could escape. On Thursday, Ms. Charles counted the club into their photo, and Samantha stood in the front row, spotless.

"Nice save," Alayna whispered, holding up two fingers crossed inside her folded sleeve. "Same time next laundry day?"

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: In Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names.
story:
Ms. Pham had set the desks in a circle and written one question on the board: "What does your name tell people about you?" Chase slouched low, because his name told people nothing interesting. It was just Chase, one syllable, and when he looked it up once, all he found was a verb meaning to run after something. Kaius went first, explaining that in his family each kid got a grandparent's name, so he carried his grandfather around whether he wanted to or not. Then Ludovic held up a get-well card his grandfather had mailed from Hungary after a surgery, and passed it around the circle. "He signed it Nagy Ludovic," Ludovic said. "Backwards. He's getting old, and I think maybe he mixed it up."

Chase turned the card over in his hands. The signature looped across the bottom in careful pen: Nagy Ludovic. At lunch he had watched Ludovic stuff the card into his backpack looking genuinely worried, and it had bothered him all afternoon. A man who had written in that same tidy hand all his life did not usually flip his own name by accident. There had to be a rule underneath it, something he couldn't see directly. He made an inference: if the grandfather's brain were failing, other things on the card would be scrambled too, like the address or the date. He checked the postmark, the street name, the small message above the signature, "Get well soon, my boy." Everything else was exact. Only the name order looked wrong to him.

Then he noticed something. Kaius's family name was Park, and Kaius always complained that teachers in books and movies put it last, when his grandfather wrote Park Kaius, family name first, in Korean. Ludovic's grandfather had done the same thing with a Hungarian name. Chase raised his hand so fast his chair scraped. "Ms. Pham, I think Ludovic's grandfather didn't make a mistake. Kaius's grandfather writes his name the same way, family name first. Hungarian might work like Korean."

Ms. Pham let the class sit with that for a second, then nodded once. "That's right. In Hungarian, the family name is written before the given name, the same order used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names."

"So he was doing it the proper way," Ludovic said slowly, "the whole time." His face went from pale to something brighter, like the lush hanging plants by the window when the sun finally swings around to them. He pulled the card from his backpack again and set it flat on his desk, tracing the signature with one finger. "I was going to ask my mom if we should call the doctor about him. I'm glad I didn't."

"You should frame it," Kaius said.

Ludovic grinned and held the card up to the light. "I'm going to hang it above my desk, exactly the way he signed it."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A tomato is botanically a fruit, but in 1893 the US Supreme Court ruled in Nix v. Hedden that it counted as a vegetable for import taxes.
story:
Anthony had been watching the same green lump on his tomato plant for six days, and on Saturday morning it finally blushed red.

"Keegan!" he shouted over the fence. "Get over here. The first one turned."

Keegan arrived with Philip close behind, both still holding half-eaten toast. They crouched around the raised bed Anthony had built from scrap boards in April. Lettuce, radishes, one optimistic cucumber vine, and three tomato plants, but only this one had produced anything ripe.

"So are we picking it or not?" Philip asked. "Because if we pick it, we eat it, and that's final."

"Cut it, don't pull it," Anthony said, and he did, holding the tomato up like a trophy.

Keegan squinted at it. "Weird to think we planted a fruit, basically an apple with delusions."

"It's a vegetable," Philip said. "That's why it's in a vegetable garden, genius."

"It grows from a flower and has seeds inside. That's fruit rules."

Anthony turned the tomato in his hand. He had never actually thought about it. He knew about seeds, and he knew Keegan's mom argued about this kind of thing at the farmers' market, but he wanted proof, not shouting. "Okay, hold on," he said. "Don't eat the evidence." He sprinted inside, grabbed his phone, and typed fast.

The search results made him laugh out loud. "You're both wrong and both right. It's a fruit, botanically. But get this. In 1893, the US Supreme Court ruled in Nix versus Hedden that it counts as a vegetable for import taxes."

"Parliament made that up?" Philip asked.

"Not parliament. The Supreme Court. Different country, different whole system." Anthony scrolled a little more. "Nix versus Hedden. It's right here."

"Clarify one thing," Keegan said. "It IS a fruit but the court SAID vegetable?"

"For taxes. That's all. So the seed people and the tax people disagree forever." Anthony held the tomato out to Philip. "You win the garden argument. He wins the science one."

Philip looked ready to gloat, but Ms. Shevchenko leaned over the hedge between the yards, watering can in hand. "Did I hear the words Nix versus Hedden in a backyard on a Saturday?"

"You know it?" Anthony said.

"My tomatoes went to a market stand once, and two vendors nearly came to blows over it," she said. "Fruit side versus vegetable side. Loud, but nobody was arrested."

Philip grinned. "So it's the most dangerous fruit in the yard."

"Only fruit in the yard," Keegan said.

"Exactly. That makes it the most vulnerable," Philip said, and snapped a bite before anyone could stop him. Juice ran down his chin.

"That was the evidence," Anthony said.

"Verdict: delicious," said Philip, and reached for the second tomato, which wasn't even ripe yet.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The Japanese word origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper.
story:
Owen spread his paper squares across the library table and tried to remember where the first fold went. The origami club met every Saturday morning in the corner by the big windows, and today he was attempting a crane, which kept turning into something that resembled a crumpled napkin.

"It's broken," Farhan said, leaning over. "That wing is not a wing."

"It's subjective," Owen said. "You can't prove it isn't a wing."

Daniyal held up his own crane, which was perfect. "Mine flew across the room yesterday. Well, I threw it. Same thing, basically."

Then the argument started. Farhan claimed that origami was a Japanese word meaning "the art of paper birds," because birds were the most common thing to fold. Daniyal said no, it meant "paper folding" in general, and that the word had nothing to do with birds at all. They looked at Owen to settle it.

Owen did not actually know. He suspected Daniyal was right, but suspicion was not proof, so he raised his hand for Ms. Nguyen, the librarian who ran the club. She was restocking the craft shelf and came over wiping dust from her hands.

"I can't just tell you," she said. "That would end the argument too fast. But there's a dictionary of Japanese loanwords in the reference section, and I believe it's on the second shelf. The one with the green cover."

Owen found the book. He had never thought about how you could take a word apart like a machine to see what was inside, but there it was, printed in black and white. He read the entry twice, then a third time to be sure, because if he was going to declare a winner, he wanted to document it properly. He copied the words onto a scrap of paper and carried it back to the table like evidence.

"Origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper," he announced. "So it just means folding paper. Nothing about birds."

Daniyal pumped his fist. Farhan frowned at his lopsided swan and said, "Fine, but my bird is still origami, so I was half right."

"You were zero halves right," said Daniyal, "but your bird is nice."

At the end of the session, Ms. Nguyen passed out index cards and said that everyone who finished a model should leave a note for next week's club members, explaining what they had made and how it had gone. Owen thought about it while he flattened his crane's wings. He wrote slowly, choosing the words.

To whoever sits at this table next Saturday: I made this crane. It took four tries. A crane that looks like a squashed frog is still origami, because the word only means folding paper, not folding it well. If yours looks better than mine, that's subjective. Also, if Farhan tells you a simile about it, like "it looks like a dying pigeon," do not listen to him.

He propped the card against his crane and set both by the window, where the afternoon light caught the paper wings. Farhan read the note over his shoulder and laughed so loudly that Ms. Nguyen raised one finger to her lips, though she was smiling too.

"Three tries," Farhan whispered, correcting the card. "You only think it was four."

"It was four," Owen said, and turned the crane to face the room.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen developed the plaster-of-Paris bandage for setting broken bones and published his method in 1852.
story:
Hazel sat on the low wall by the swings with her left arm propped in her lap, the new white cast already smudged with gray from the wall's bricks. Two days ago she had slipped off the monkey bars, and now the whole playground felt like a different place, a place she could only watch. The one thing she could still do was sign casts. Jewel crouched beside her with a green marker, drawing a tiny frog on the plaster.

"Wait," said Gideon, dropping onto the wall on her other side. "Before you draw on it, shouldn't you pick a color? My cousin got to choose. She got purple." He tapped Hazel's cast. "Why is yours just white?"

"Mr. Sok picked it because it was fastest," Hazel said. "The nurse said colored ones take longer to get from the supply room." She turned the frog toward the sun. "Anyway, I like white. It's like a blank page."

Gideon frowned at it. "But how did people even fix broken arms before casts existed? They must have just... hopelessly flopped around."

Hazel started to say she didn't know, then stopped. She had seen something in the library that morning, a page she had flipped past in a medical book while waiting for the dismissal bell. "Actually, there was a guy," she said slowly, working it back into order. "A Dutch army surgeon. Antonius Mathijsen. He developed a bandage made of plaster of Paris, the stuff for setting broken bones, and he published his method in 1852."

"Plaster of Paris?" Jewel said. "Like what we used for the volcano project?"

"Same stuff, I think." Hazel knocked on her cast with her knuckle and it answered with a dull, stony knock back. "So before 1852, everything was different, and after, this." She held up her arm like evidence.

Gideon looked skeptical, which was his usual setting. "You're saying your arm is wrapped in volcano paste because of one army surgeon? That sounds like something you half remember."

Hazel's face went warm. She hated being told she half remembered things, especially when she might have half remembered them. "Fine," she said. "Test me. Mr. Sok's door is right there, and he has that big medical dictionary on his shelf. If I'm wrong, you can ridicule me for a week. If I'm right, you have to sign the cast with the frog, right on its back."

Mr. Sok was on yard duty by the fence, and he let them crowd into his doorway during the break. He pulled the dictionary down, licked his thumb, and turned pages while three heads leaned in under his elbow. There it was, under a small entry about bandages. Gideon read it out loud in a flat voice, as if the words were being pulled out of him one at a time: Dutch army surgeon Antonius Mathijsen, plaster of Paris, published his method in 1852.

"Okay," Gideon said. "You win. I change my mind about the white, too. It's not boring, it's historical." He took the green marker from Jewel and wrote his name in careful letters along the frog's back. "There. Part of the ecosystem of your arm now."

"Everything on this playground is an ecosystem," Jewel said, shading the frog's eye. "And casting arms became mandatory for people who fall off monkey bars, apparently."

"That rule is definitely real," Hazel said, and tucked her arm against her side, the ink still wet, the green signature shining.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: On the Holmes and Rahe stress scale, published in 1967, both changing residence and changing schools are listed as life events that require readjustment.
story:
The new house smelled like paint and nothing else. Lea stood in the middle of her empty bedroom, where her voice bounced off the walls in a way that felt too loud, and read the message on her phone again. It was from Chiara, sent that morning: "Day 3 without you. The cafeteria gave me two milks because the cashier thought I was you. I drank both. Hope you're surviving."

Lea typed a reply, deleted it, and typed another one. "Surviving is an approximate word for it. My room has zero posters, one box, and an echo." Then she wandered downstairs, past the movers' tape lines on the floor, and out the front door to the porch, where the neighbor lady was arranging pots of basil along her steps like soldiers.

"New house," the neighbor said, in a tone that could have meant welcome or could have meant get off my lawn. "You'll feel worse than you expect for a while. It's not a mystery." She held up a paperback with a cracked spine. "Holmes and Rade, 1967. Stress scale. Changing residence, changing schools, both on the list. Life events that require readjustment." Then she went inside and shut the door, leaving Lea on the steps with the basil and the strange certainty that the woman had been waiting weeks to say that to somebody.

Lea sat down to test it, because that was what she did when something sounded too neat. If moving house and switching schools both counted as readjustment events, then she was doing two of them at once, which meant feeling terrible on day four was not evidence that something was wrong with her. She needed a second data point. She texted Naila, who had moved in fourth grade: "Did you feel weird after your move, like, hormonally and every other way?" Naila wrote back, "I cried over a missing sock for a week and blamed my hormones. My mom said it was the move. Why?" Lea sent back, "Science. I'll explain Monday when the internet people come." She felt something loosen in her chest, the way a room loosens when you open a window and let the light saturate every corner that had gone gray.

She thought about the choice she and her parents had made back in March, sitting at the kitchen table with the map spread out, when she had said moving was fine. Some days she still thought it was fine. Other days she missed Chiara's two-milk cashier so much it hurt, and she let both of those opinions sit side by side without choosing between them. On Monday she would unpack the box marked POSTERS FIRST, because Ms. Pritchard had a name after all, printed on her mail slot, and because even readjustment events deserved a decorated room. For now, Lea carried one basil leaf home from the neighbor's steps, set it in a glass of water on the windowsill, and said out loud to the empty house, "You're welcome."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: On a graph, a simple-interest balance rises in a straight line, while a compound-interest balance curves upward, gaining more each year than the year before.
story:
Livia stood outside the electronics store with her nose almost touching the glass, staring at the silver headphones that refract the mall lights like tiny mirrors. "Two hundred dollars," she said. "I have sixty. My birthday money is going into the bank Saturday, and I'm choosing an account that actually gets me there faster."

Colin groaned. "It's the mall. We're supposed to be eating pretzels."

"Two minutes." Livia pulled the folded bank flyer out of her jacket. "Look, two options. Simple interest, or compound interest, for five years. My mom says just pick one, but I want to know which one wins." She jabbed the paper. "The problem is you can't see interest. It's invisible. It just happens in the bank's computer."

"Then guess," said Alana, already drifting toward the pretzel smell.

"No, I can test it." Livia grabbed a napkin from the food court, borrowed Colin's pen, and drew two axes right next to a tray of half-eaten fries. She plotted the simple interest first, year by year, and the points fell into a perfectly straight line, climbing the same amount every single year, steady and consistent, like stairs. "Okay, that one behaves." Then she plotted the compound one, and her pen slowed down. The first few points hugged the straight line so closely she almost thought they matched. But by year three the compound points pulled above it, and by year five they had curved sharply upward, leaping higher each year than the year before, like the line itself was getting excited. "Wait. Wait wait wait. Look at this."

Colin leaned over, a pretzel suspended halfway to his mouth. "The curvy one wins?"

"By a lot, at the end. It gains more every year than the year before. The straight one never changes its mind." Alana grabbed the pen and connected the dots herself, and the curve bent upward under her hand like a ramp.

Mr. Nasser, who ran the phone-repair kiosk next door, wandered over out of curiosity. He squinted at the napkin, chuckled, and said, "You drew compound interest curving up and simple interest going straight? That's exactly right. Customers ask me about savings all the time, and nobody ever draws it."

Livia smoothed the napkin flat, folded it with the care of someone holding treasure, and slid it into her back pocket. "Saturday, bank, compound," she announced, and then pointed at the headphones. "Five years, and those are mine." Colin handed her the last pretzel, and she took a victory bite.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: In a 1974 study by Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, people who were asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked about cars that 'hit.'
story:
At four o'clock on Tuesdays, the science club took over Mr. García's classroom, and this Tuesday Kaitlyn marched in carrying her notebook like it was evidence for a trial. On Friday, two seventh graders had collided in the hallway by the water fountain, and ever since, the story had been splitting into pieces. Rami swore one of them was running full speed. Safa insisted they had barely bumped at all. Kaitlyn wanted to know which of them was right, because she was planning to write the whole thing up for the club's newsletter and she refused to print a guess.

"Here's what I don't get," she said, dropping into the seat between them. "You were both standing right there. It's not like one of you was in the bathroom."

"I'm telling you, they smashed into each other," Rami said, slapping his palms together for effect. "Like, ten miles an hour, minimum."

"Ten miles an hour is jogging," Safa said. "Nobody jogs in that hallway, not even Devon, and Devon jogs everywhere. They hit, sure. It was more of a glide."

Kaitlyn wrote smashed and hit in her notebook and underlined both. Then a memory floated up, something she wished she could un-remember. Last month she had knocked over her mom's lamp, and when her mom asked, gentle and worried, "Did it just tip, or did it smash?", Kaitlyn had heard herself say "smash" even though the lamp had done no such thing. She had spent a week feeling guilty about the word choice, and about the look on her mom's face. Maybe people's words leaked into other people's memories. Maybe the question itself was doing something.

"I have a theory," she announced, "and it needs an experiment." She found two sixth graders by the door, both of whom had also seen the hallway collision. She asked the first one, "How fast were they going when they hit each other?" and the second one, "How fast were they going when they smashed into each other?" The first kid said slow, kind of a shuffle. The second kid said fast, definitely fast, maybe even faster than Devon. Same collision. Same hallway. Two different verbs going in, two different speeds coming out.

Mr. García leaned against his desk, listening. "You've stumbled onto something," he said. "In 1974, two researchers, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer, found exactly that. People asked how fast cars smashed into each other gave higher speed estimates than people asked how fast cars hit."

"So Rami's word got into my head," Safa said slowly. "That is somehow the most annoying thing that has ever happened to me."

"It means nobody lied," Kaitlyn said. "We integrate what we hear into what we remember, and we can't even feel it happening." She looked down at her notebook, where the word "smash" sat underlined twice, looking, she thought, a little toxic now, like it had poisoned her data on purpose. "Safa, when I asked you about it at lunch, I probably said smashed, didn't I?"

Safa nodded. "Right before you stole my fries. So on some level, this is your fault."

Kaitlyn laughed, then flipped to a clean page. Her compassion for Rami had gone way up; her guilt about the lamp had gone way down, which felt strange and comfortable at the same time. "New headline for the newsletter," she said. "'The Hallway Crash That Nobody Actually Misremembered.'"

"Terrible headline," said Rami.

"Fine. You write it. But I get to pick the verb."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: The Galápagos finches have beaks suited to different foods, such as thin beaks for picking insects and deep, heavy beaks for cracking hard seeds.
story:
Rachel had exactly eleven minutes to figure out the finch station before Mr. Demetriou's quiz, and the finches were not cooperating.

The station was a table in the science museum's evolution hall. On one side sat six rubbery finch heads, each with a different beak: one thin as a tweezers, one deep and heavy as a nutcracker, and four somewhere in between. On the other side sat a tray of foods: hard seeds like tiny rocks, soft little insects pickled in a jar, a berry, some kind of pulp. A sign said MATCH EACH BEAK TO ITS FOOD. Aksil had already matched three, and he was wrong about all three, which he announced with total confidence.

"Big beak eats the berry," Aksil said. "Big beak, big food."

"That's not a rule," Rachel said. "That's a guess with attitude." She picked up the deep, heavy beak model and turned it over. It looked like it could crack things. She set it in front of the hard seeds and pressed down gently. The seed split clean in half. Then she took the thin beak, the tweezers one, and tried it on a seed. Nothing. It slid off. She dipped it toward the jar and found it could slide right between the pickled insects and pick one up like a fork tine. "Okay," she said. "Thin beak, insects. Heavy beak, hard seeds."

Bilal wandered over from the volcano exhibit, chewing the string of his hoodie. "So the finches just got the beaks they wanted?"

"They didn't order them off a menu," Rachel said. She lined up the remaining beaks between the berry, the pulp, and the medium seeds, working by size, testing each one against a food like a locksmith trying keys. Aksil kept trying to grab the deep beak for the berry, and she kept sliding it back. "You don't get a monopoly on the answers just because you're louder," she said.

"I'm being pessimistic," Aksil said. "That's different."

Mr. Demetriou appeared behind them with his clipboard. "So," he said. "Evaluate your matches. Why would insects and seeds need different beaks at all?"

Rachel looked down the row she had built, thin to heavy, soft food to hard food. "The food does it," she said slowly. "The beaks suit what's there to eat. On one island there's bugs, on another there's big tough seeds, so..." She stopped, because the whole line of beaks suddenly looked like an answer instead of a puzzle.

Mr. Demetriou wrote something on his clipboard and said nothing, which was somehow worse than a quiz.

Rachel slid the tweezers beak forward, picked up the last insect, and held it out to Aksil. "You try."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
story:
Aurora stood at the edge of the parking lot, where the school had set up the dance under a canopy between two light poles. Lilya and River were already underneath, and a mirror ball hung from a crossbar above the refreshment table. Aurora had heard that the dance committee bought it secondhand because a new imported one cost extra after the tariff, so nobody minded the chips in it.

She was working up the nerve to walk over and ask Lilya to save her a dance when the music started and the chaperone, Ms. Morningstar, switched on the single spotlight on its stand. The ball spun, and hundreds of small spots of light swept across the pavement, sliding over car doors and River's sneakers. Hundreds of spots from one spotlight. Aurora had assumed the ball glowed somehow, but it was plugged into nothing. It hung on a rope. The light had to be bouncing off it, and if each little mirror tile on the ball tilted a slightly different way, each one would throw the beam in a slightly different direction. That would explain the hundreds of spots, all moving as the ball turned.

She could test that. She stepped into the path of the light near the wall and raised one hand to cover a single tile on the ball's edge. One spot on the pavement went dark. When she moved her hand, it came back. So one tile made one spot.

Then River tripped on the spotlight cord and the beam swung away from the ball. The whole parking lot went to flat yellow from the streetlights, and everyone groaned. "It's broken," Lilya said. Aurora said, "No, the ball just isn't catching the beam anymore." She righted the stand and aimed the spotlight at the ball until the spots came back and crawled across the cars again.

Ms. Morningstar, who had been unlocking her car for the box of extra sodas, called out, "Good fix." The committee had voted unanimously for the mirror ball over a rented fog machine, and now Aurora could see why. River gave the ball a slow spin with one finger, and the spots ran in long streaks across the asphalt and up the chain-link fence.

Lilya came over and stood beside her in the moving light. "You've been hiding by the cars this whole time?"

"Figuring out how the ball works," Aurora said. "It's one spotlight, not hundreds."

Lilya held out her hand. "Then come stand in them with me."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: One-point perspective works when you face straight down a street, so the fronts of objects face you and everything else recedes to one point.
story:
On the second day of art camp, Ms. Khan handed out pencils and announced that the afternoon project was a city street, drawn in one-point perspective. "The lines meet at a vanishing point," Kamden whispered to Georgia, as if sharing a secret about a marsupial nobody else had spotted. Georgia nodded like she understood, which was generous of her.

Her drawing refused to cooperate. She had copied the idea faithfully: edges of buildings slanting inward toward a single dot, sidewalks narrowing, everything rushing toward that one point on her paper. Yet her street looked like it had been folded in half by a tired origami artist. Kamden leaned over, studied the wreckage, and said, "Mine looks like that too, but worse." This was somehow comforting.

Georgia wanted to figure out the problem herself, mostly because asking Ms. Khan felt like admitting her artistic talent might not be hereditary, however often her grandmother claimed otherwise. She walked out to the gravel road that ran past the mess hall and stood at the corner where the camp's two paths crossed. Facing down the left path, she noticed that the fronts of the cabins directly ahead stared straight back at her, flat and plain, while their side walls squeezed toward one spot far ahead. She held up her pencil, squinting along the edge of the nearest cabin like an artist in a movie, and it all lined up. One path, one point.

Then she turned to face the corner itself, where both paths met at an angle, and tried the same trick. The pencil lines disagreed with each other. The left path's edges wanted to converge in one direction, the right path's in another, like two friends arguing about which trail to take. Her drawing, she realized with a small hot flash of annoyance, was a corner view pretending to be a straight one. No wonder it looked folded.

Back inside, she started over. She drew the street as if she were standing in the middle of it, dead center, staring straight down its length. The building fronts faced her like flat postcards, and everything else receded to that single dot. Kamden watched the new drawing take shape and frowned at his own paper. "How'd you do that?"

"I stopped drawing a corner," Georgia said, and picked up her eraser to make the old attempt evaporate.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A traditional corded phone on a copper landline usually keeps working in a power cut, because the phone company powers the line, but cordless phones need household electricity.
story:
The lights in Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya's kitchen ceased their flickering and went out all at once, and Emily, who had been borrowing the counter to finish her science homework, was left staring at a page she could no longer read. The whole street outside had gone dark too, house by house, like someone walking along switching off the world.

"Ice cream in the freezer will survive an hour," Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya said from the hallway, her voice calm in the way of someone who had lived through many such evenings. "The candles are in the drawer under the oven. Mind the corner table, it is older than my grandmother's dynasty and twice as wobbly."

Emily found the candles, and also Kiaan from next door, who had seen the dark street and come over because his house had no candles at all. They set two candles on the counter and watched the flames lean whenever anyone breathed. "I was going to call my mom and tell her I'm here," Kiaan said, picking up the phone from its charging stand. He pressed the button and held it to his ear, then pressed it again. "Nothing. Not even the little screen."

Emily took the dead handset and turned it over in her hands. It was plastic and light, with buttons that normally glowed. Now it was just a shell. She looked at the wall socket where the charger was plugged in, and a wondering question began to form: if the phone itself was fine, and the socket had no power, then what exactly had stopped? She said it out loud, because saying things out loud sometimes made them clearer. "The phone's not broken. The electricity is broken. So does the phone need the electricity?"

"Everything needs electricity," Kiaan said.

But Emily was already scanning the kitchen, and her eyes landed on something low on the far wall, half hidden behind a stack of recipe books: an old phone, the dilapidated kind with a curly cord and a dial you had to drag around with your finger. It looked like it belonged in a museum. "That one doesn't plug into anything," she said slowly. "Except the phone line." She crossed the kitchen, lifted the heavy receiver, and pressed it to her ear.

There was a hum, then a small, crisp dial tone, steady and alive in the dark room.

"It's working," she said. "Kiaan, the old one still works." He hurried over and listened, his eyebrows going up. Emily handed him the receiver. "Call your mom. Tell her you're here, and tell her the cordless phones are dead but this one isn't." Then she stood there in the candlelight, holding the old cord in her hand, following its loops with her finger and grinning. "Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya, I'm keeping this phone forever."

"Then you had better wind the cord around it," Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya called from the hallway, "before the cat decides it is a toy."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
story:
Jessica had the health poster flat on the kitchen table, smoothing out the creases with both palms, when her mother called from the hallway that the dishes were still her job tonight.

"Five more minutes," Jessica said, though she had already been at the table for twenty.

The poster had come down outside Mr. Flores's classroom, where it had hung since September. According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, it read in bold blue letters, mental health includes a person's emotional, psychological and social well-being. Jessica had walked past it a hundred times without stopping. Today she had stopped, because of Nicholas.

He had not answered her messages in four days. Before that, he had sat with her and Fatimah at lunch every day since third grade, and now he was at the end table with his headphones on, hunched like a closing door. Fatimah said to leave him alone. Jessica had said maybe that was respect, giving him space, and she'd felt virtuous about it right up until this afternoon, when Nicholas had looked over at their table and then looked away so fast it hurt to watch. Now she couldn't stop speculating. Had space helped, or had it just felt like nobody cared?

She traced the poster's three words with her finger. Emotional. Psychological. Social. The social one snagged on her like a sleeve on a nail. She had always pictured mental health as something that happened inside one person, like a toothache. But if the social part counted too, then friendships were part of Nicholas's health, the way sleep was part of his health. Leaving him alone might not be coping. It might be the opposite.

Fatimah arrived at four, still holding her bike helmet, because Jessica had texted her come over NOW and Fatimah knew what capital letters meant.

"So you think we've been doing it wrong," Fatimah said, turning the poster toward herself. "The whole give-him-space plan."

"I don't know. But we never tested it. We just decided." Jessica pulled out her phone. "One message. Not ten. If he doesn't answer, that's a boundary, and we respect it. But we never even knocked."

The message said, Miss you at lunch. Door's open whenever. Jessica sent it, then wiped the table with vigorous, unnecessary strokes while the phone sat silent between them. Fatimah ate an apple. The kitchen clock got louder.

At 4:31 the phone buzzed. The reply was short: Door open tomorrow?

Jessica held the screen out so Fatimah could read it, and Fatimah said, "So it was the not-knocking," and Jessica said, "Maybe," because she still wasn't sure where the line was between helping and crowding, and she suspected she wouldn't be sure for a long time.

"Either way," she said, sliding the poster into her backpack, "I'm asking him where he got the headphones."

Fatimah laughed so hard she dropped the apple core, and Jessica picked it up and shot it into the trash can from across the kitchen.

activity: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
knowledge_domain: to prove two triangles congruent using the side-angle-side rule
fact: Vertical angles, the opposite angles formed when two straight lines cross, are always equal, which often supplies the angle needed for side-angle-side.
story:
Arthur sat at the kitchen table glaring at his geometry homework like it was a carnivore about to bite. The page showed two triangles sharing a crossing point, an X shape where their sides overlapped, and the instructions demanded that he prove the triangles congruent. He had two pairs of sides marked equal, tick marks on the little line segments, but the rule written in his notes said side-angle-side. Two sides alone would not do it. He needed an angle between them, and the diagram gave him nothing.

Rosie had texted him three times already, asking whether he had finished, because Ms. Swampy was collecting the assignment first thing and had promised a zero for anyone who guessed. Arthur texted back "still working" and slid his phone face down. His pencil tapped the paper. He tried redrawing the triangles in the margin, pulling them apart so they stood alone, but when he did, the crossing point disappeared and took his only hope with it. The desk lamp buzzed. Outside the window the yard lay barren under the streetlight, no distractions anywhere, no excuse to get up.

He turned the page sideways, then upside down, hunting for anything marked equal. Then he stopped. He leaned close to the X, so close his breath fogged the paper. The angle he needed, the one wedged between his two marked sides on the first triangle, sat right at the crossing. So did an angle on the second triangle, directly opposite it, across the intersection. He grabbed his ruler and extended both lines with careful strokes. They were straight. Completely straight, each one.

"Wait," he said out loud to the empty kitchen.

He remembered Ms. Swampy saying the words once, fast, near the end of class while everyone was packing up. Vertical angles, she had called them, the opposite angles formed when two straight lines cross, and they are always equal. Arthur felt his pulse thump. If these two angles were vertical angles, then the angle he needed was hiding directly across the crossing point, already equal, no measuring required.

But he would not trust his memory alone. He took a scrap of paper, drew a fresh X, and measured both opposite angles with his protractor. Equal. He drew another, crooked on purpose. Equal again. He spent ten minutes verifying it, then wrote his proof in careful steps: the sides were given, the angles were vertical angles and therefore equal, so by side-angle-side the triangles were congruent.

His phone buzzed. Rosie: "Did you figure it out or are we both doomed?"

Arthur picked it up and grinned at the ceiling.

"Come over," he typed. "Bring your protractor. I found where the angle was hiding."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see.
story:
Mathis had promised Ms. Diallo a labelled diagram of onion cells by Monday, and so far his notebook contained one drawing of a very pale nothing. The microscope sat on the picnic table in his backyard, borrowed from the school science room, along with a box of slides, a dropper bottle, and an onion his dad had donated from the kitchen without being asked.

The hard part was getting the sample. Onion skin was thin, but it did not want to come off in the thin, flat sheet the instructions demanded. Mathis cut the onion in half, pried apart a layer with tweezers, and tried to excavate the papery skin from the inside curve without tearing it. It took four tries and some stinging eyes. Beside him, Madelynn held the tweezers like a winning lottery ticket, with the fifth.

"I got a whole piece," she announced. "No holes. Not even a small one."

They laid the skin flat in a drop of water on the slide, lowered the cover slip, and Mathis leaned in. He turned the focus knob slowly, the way Ms. Diallo had shown the class, waiting for the cells to snap into view. He kept turning. What he saw was a faint grid, like a fence drawn in pencil and then mostly erased. The diagram in his textbook showed a cell wall, a membrane, and a dark nucleus in each brick-shaped cell. His slide showed bricks made of whisper.

"There's something there," he said. "Barely. I can outline the walls, I guess, but the nucleus is just not happening."

Madelynn squinted through the eyepiece for a long moment. "It's like they're invisible," she said. "Or the microscope's broken." Then she straightened up. "Wait. In class we used iodine on a potato and it turned black, because of the starch. Starch is a carbohydrate, and iodine finds it." She was already reaching into the box, past the lens paper, past the spare slides. "There's a little brown bottle in here. It says iodine."

Mathis thought about it. Onion skin cells were nearly colourless, that much was obvious from the nothing he'd been staring at. Colourless things did not show up well. If iodine turned one thing black, maybe a single drop of it would darken whatever it touched, nucleus and all. It was a simple idea, and the only one on the table.

"One drop," he said. "Right on the edge of the cover slip, so it slides under."

Madelynn's hand was steady. The drop crept along the slip, and under the lens the pale grid flushed gold-brown. Mathis turned the fine focus a quarter turn, and there they were: cell walls standing out like drawn lines, and inside each brick, a small, definite nucleus, darker than everything around it.

"Draw fast," Madelynn said, handing him the pencil. "Before it gets shy again." Mathis flipped to a clean page and began at the top left brick.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish adjectives usually come after the noun they describe, so "a black cat" is "un gato negro."
story:
Brody slid his flashcards across the desk and counted them twice. Tomorrow each student had to stand up in Spanish class and describe their family and pets in full sentences, and so far he had three cards that made sense and six that did not. Mr. Gupta had written a sample on the board: un gato negro. Brody copied it into his notebook and frowned at it, because in his head his cat was "a negro gato," and that was how he had written it on card four.

Charly leaned over from the next desk, drumming a pencil against her eraser. "I go first tomorrow," she said. "I signed up before anyone else. I want to get it over with before lunch, so I don't sit through math worrying about it." She had written her sentences about her two brothers and a goldfish, and she kept rereading them like they might change.

Brody laid his cards side by side. One said "mi hermana es alta," which Mr. Gupta had confirmed was right, tall sister. Another said "un perro grande," big dog, also right. Then he looked at his own card, "un negro gato," and back at the board, and a pattern began to form. Every correct sentence he had put the describing word second. Mi madre es simpatica. Un perro grande. Un gato negro. His wrong card was the only one where he had flipped them.

"I think Spanish puts the describing word after," Brody said slowly. He turned the card over and wrote un gato negro underneath his first attempt, then hunted through his notebook for the other pet sentences he had made. A fish, two cats. He swapped each pair and read them aloud under his breath.

"Let me hear one," Charly said.

"Tengo dos gatos gordos," Brody said. "I have two fat cats." He paused, waiting to see if it sounded backwards, but it didn't anymore. His breathing began to regulate itself as the pattern settled in, and his ears stopped burning. "And un perro blanco. A white dog."

Charly copied his fixes onto her own cards, then flipped one over and showed him. "What about this one? Mi pez es anaranjado."

"Describing word at the end," Brody said. "You're fine."

At the end of class Mr. Gupta walked between the rows, dry as the arid air outside, and stopped at Brody's desk. "Read me one sentence about your family," he said.

Brody picked up the card about his sister and the one about his cats and read them both without stopping once. Mr. Gupta nodded and moved on.

Charly raised her hand before anyone else could. "Tomorrow, I'm still going first," she said.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Simon had promised his grandfather he would learn one full song on the old piano by Thanksgiving, and the piano sat in the garage because his mother said it would never fit through the front door. Every afternoon he dragged a stool across the cold concrete and practiced while the smell of motor oil drifted around him. The trouble was that the song kept sounding wrong, and he could not figure out why.

His friend Arie came over after school, mostly because Arie wanted to turn the garage's back corner into a skate wax workshop, which Simon's mother had flatly refused. "Your house is the rebellion headquarters now," Arie said, dropping his backpack on a stack of paint cans. "My parents say my room smells like a factory."

"Listen to this," Simon said, and played the first eight bars. The notes were right. He had checked them a dozen times against the sheet music propped on a lawn chair. But the melody came out crooked, like a staircase with one step missing.

Arie listened with his chin in his hands. "It sounds kind of lopsided. Like you're landing hard on some notes and skipping others."

That was it, Simon realized. He wasn't skipping anything, but he was landing in the wrong places, and he could not see the pattern from the page alone. He needed to know the ground he was standing on. He ran his fingers along the keys and started counting, tapping each one with a pencil eraser so he wouldn't lose his place. White keys: fifty-two. Black keys: thirty-six. He counted twice to be sure, then added them in his head. Eighty-eight keys in all, and every single one of them a place his fingers could land wrong.

So he tested an idea. He put a strip of blue painter's tape along the edge of one key, the C where the melody began, so his hand would have a landmark instead of guessing. Then he played the eight bars again, watching the tape instead of the page. The melody came out even, step after step, all the way to the final note.

From the driveway, Ms. Ahmed called through the gap under the garage door, "That sounded almost like actual music today, Simon."

"It was actual music," Simon said, grinning.

Arie was already negotiating with him, offering to hold the flashlight every afternoon after dark if Simon would let him build one small shelf in the corner, somewhere out of sight, where his wax could live. Simon thought about it. The garage was technically the most affluent room in the house now, what with a piano in it, and a shelf seemed like a fair price for a flashlight holder.

He peeled off the tape, smoothed it back down, and started the song again from the top.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part of the quote begins with a lowercase letter because the sentence is continuing.
story:
Bentley slid his draft across the table toward Hareem and Diya, pencil already in his fist. Writing club met in Ms. Clarke's room every Thursday, and today was the day everyone shared a story with dialogue in it.

"Read mine out loud," he said. "I want to hear it."

Hareem picked it up. "'We need to leave now,' Mom said. 'Before the tide comes in.'" She frowned. "Wait, that sounds like two separate things she said."

"It is two things," Bentley said. But when he heard it, the rhythm felt wrong, like a hiccup in the middle. He leaned over the page. The first part, the second part, the tag stuck between them. He tapped his pencil. "Or is it one thing?"

Diya leaned in, and her grin was infectious. "Try crossing out 'Mom said' and reading the quote straight through."

Bentley covered the tag with his thumb. "We need to leave now before the tide comes in." His pencil froze. One sentence. The tag had just interrupted it, like someone stepping between two friends walking down a hall. He erased the capital B and wrote "before" with a lowercase letter. "The second part is still the same sentence," he said. "So it doesn't get a capital."

"Let's assume that works every time the tag splits one sentence," Hareem said, flipping through her own draft. She found a split quote, tested it with her thumb the same way, and lowered her second capital too.

Ms. Clarke stopped at their table and read Bentley's page. "Now you have a candidate for the read-aloud at the end of club," she said. "Your story has a climax, too, that wave hitting the cave roof. Read it to everyone."

Bentley stood up so fast his chair squeaked. He read the whole story aloud, and when he reached the fixed line, it flowed the way he had heard it in his head. The tide roared, the flashlight died, and Mom's voice cut through the dark, all in one breath. The other kids clapped.

That night he wrote his grandmother a letter, because she had asked him what club he kept racing off to every week.

Dear Grandma,

You will not believe what happened today. I learned that when a dialogue tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part of the quote starts with a lowercase letter, because the sentence is continuing. I found it out myself, with a thumb over the tag. Ms. Clarke picked my cave story for the read-aloud. I am going to write you a whole story next week, dialogue and all.

Love, Bentley

He sealed the envelope, grabbed his flashlight, and ran to the mailbox at the corner before the mail truck came.
